## Paper

## Abstract

Recently, superconductivity with onset transition temperature (T onset) over 40 K was achieved in La3Ni2O7 and (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films at ambient pressure due to in-plane compressive strain. However, the Tc in these thin films are lower than that of the bulk bilayer nickelates under pressure. Here we report the enhancement of T onset from about 30 K to over 48 K by applying hydrostatic pressure on the compressively strained bilayer nickelate thin films. The T onset firstly ramps up with pressure, then it slightly drops down after reaching the maximum T onset at about 48.5 K. Our theoretical calculations yield a cooperative enhancement of magnetic fluctuations between and within the layers and increased metallicity under pressure. These findings highlight the critical role of the interplay between interlayer and intralayer electronic correlations in bilayer nickelate superconductors and point to the potential of tuning Tc through controlled manipulation of the electronic structure and interactions.

---

## Introduction

The discovery of superconductivity in bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 with transition temperature (Tc) exceeding the boiling temperature of liquid nitrogen has drawn enormous attention in both theoretical and experimental studies in the past 2 years. The electronic configuration in bilayer nickelate system is 3d7.5 (Ni2.5+) with dominantly the contributions of the eg orbitals, namely the 3d x2-y2 and 3d z2 orbitals near the Fermi level. Nowadays, nickelate superconductors are regarded as a new type of unconventional high-Tc superconductor beside the cuprates and lron-based superconductors. However, the requirement of high-pressure conditions to achieve superconductivity in the bilayer system has inhibited the investigation of the superconducting mechanism and potential applications of nickelate superconductors. Therefore, the pursuit of superconductivity at ambient pressure in nickelates with the Ruddlesden-Popper phase has been an ongoing task, and several promising routes, such as chemical substitution or strain effect, have been proposed in previous studies. Since the superconductivity in nickelate was first observed in an infinite-layer thin film with Tc about 9–15 K at ambient pressure, it is highly desired to explore ambient pressure superconductivity in La3Ni2O7 system via strains or fine tuning of the oxygen stoichiometry. Indeed, thin films of bilayer nickelates on different substrates have already been successfully fabricated, showing a promising route to achieve ambient pressure superconductivity. Very recently, signatures of superconductivity above 40 K in bilayer nickelate with a compressive strain (about −2%) at ambient pressure is achieved in bilayer nickelate thin films grown on SrLaAlO4 (SLAO) substrate and the superconducting properties can be strongly enhanced through combined chemical substitution and precise optimization during growth and post oxidation treatment. These findings have stimulated enormous interest, and several theoretical and experimental investigations have been carried out very quickly. The angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measurements on this type of films reveal the presence of the α and β Fermi surface sheets with the mixed 3d x2-y2 and 3d z2 orbital content, but without consensus about the existence of γ pocket which is purely derived from the 3d z2 orbital. The single particle tunneling spectroscopy measurements suggest the dominance of anisotropic s-wave gap(s) in the compressively strained bilayer nickelate films, supporting the Cooper-pairing scenario of bonding-antibonding s±-wave superconductivity. However, the maximum Tc observed in bilayer nickelate thin films so far is much lower than that in bulk samples under high pressure. One possible scenario is that the large compressive strain in ab-plane not only enhances the in-plane coupling to stabilize the ambient pressure superconductivity, but also increases the lattice constant in c-axis, thereby weakening the interlayer coupling along the c direction. In bulk La3Ni2O7, the flat band (γ band) with a large density of states just below the Fermi level with dominantly 3d z2 orbital character may play the essential role for the occurrence of high-Tc superconductivity. Therefore, the Tc in bilayer films might be further enhanced through chemical substitution or adding pressure to shorten the c-axis lattice constant.

In this work, we report the enhanced superconductivity on the superconducting bilayer heterostructure of (La,Pr)3Ni2O7/(La,Sr)3Ni2O7 on SLAO(001) substrate. At ambient pressure, the Tonset of the bilayer thin films is around 30 K (determined by using the crossing method as detailed below), and the superconducting properties are pretty stable in air. By applying pressure, the Tonset is monotonically enhanced up to 48.5 K at 7 GPa. With further increasing pressure, the Tonset is saturated and decreases slowly with increasing pressure, giving a dome-shaped superconducting region. More importantly, the normal-state transport measurements above Tonset show a transition from metallic to weak insulating behavior with increasing pressure. Aided by the theoretical calculations, our results imply crucial effect of interplay of interlayer and intralayer multiorbital electronic correlations as well as the metallicity in governing the superconducting transition temperature.

---

## Results

Growth and characterization of bilayer nickelate thin films
According to the previous literatures, the superconducting bilayer nickelate thin films may have some diffusion of Sr2+ into the substrate-film interface. Therefore, to enhance the stability of the superconductivity in the films, we firstly deposit a 1.5 unit-cell (UC) of La2.85Sr0.15Ni2O7 layer on the SLAO(001) substrate, then deposit a 1.5 UC-La2.5Pr0.5Ni2O7 thin film, forming an artificial structure as illustrated by the schematic plot in Fig. 1a. The details for the growth parameters and heterostructure design can be found in Supplementary Note 1. The quality of the obtained thin film was confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) 2θ-ω scans along the (00l) direction. The XRD data are shown in Fig. 1b. All the diffraction peaks from the films can be well indexed by the bilayer structure with the c-axis lattice constant of about 20.78 Å. This value is in good agreement with the previous studies on bilayer thin films and slightly elongated (+1.5%) compared to the bulk La3Ni2O7 (~20.45 Å) samples at ambient pressure. We also measured the Reciprocal space mapping (RSM) around the bilayer thin films (1017) and SLAO (1011) reflections (see Supplementary Fig. 1a), which confirm that the film is coherently attached to the substrate and thus compressively strained, with an in-plane lattice constant of about 3.75 Å. These results indicate that the film is compressively strained (−2%) in plane by the substrate, but the c-axis lattice constant elongates a little bit. By fabricating the (La,Pr)3Ni2O7/(La,Sr)3Ni2O7 heterostructure (LSP327) with a compressive strain and precise in-situ ozone annealing, we can obtain superconducting nickelate thin films with the bilayer structure. Interestingly, our films are quite stable in air, which maybe induced by the specially designed heterostructure (see Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2).

Figure 1d displays the temperature dependent resistivity ρ(T) of a variety of thin films. All the measured thin films exhibit good metallic behavior and clear superconducting transitions at ambient pressure. The Tonset varies from 21 to 34 K and most of the transitions have a resistivity drop over 90% at 2 K. In this paper, we define the onset of superconducting transition (Tonset) as the cross-point of the linear extrapolation of normal state and the transition region with 80–90% of the normal-state resistivity. We also measured the ρ(T) curves for LSP327 films under different applied magnetic fields (see Supplementary Fig. 1b). The resistivity transitions are gradually pushed to lower temperatures by magnetic field as expected for a superconducting transition. The magnetic field dependent Hall resistance (RH) of LSP327 thin film was measured between 40 and 200 K (see Supplementary Fig. 3) by using the standard five-probe method on the thin film with a size of 3 mm × 1.5 mm as shown in the inset of Fig. 1c. Since the sample size is relatively large with a rectangular shape, and the electrodes for applying the current is parallelly made in the two terminals, therefore, the current is supposed to be uniformly applied on the thin films. As shown in Fig. 1c, the calculated Hall coefficient (RH) is positive at measured temperatures and decreases with increasing temperature. Such behavior may indicate the multiband nature or correlation effect of the superconducting bilayer nickelate thin films in the normal state, and is consistent with previous results on bulk crystals and undoped La3Ni2O7 thin films. Note that a negative RH was observed in some doped bilayer nickelate thin films previously and an electron-hole crossover of the RH was reported in superconducting La3-xSrxNi2O7-δ thin films with different oxygen content. Therefore, the positive RH in our bilayer LSP327 thin film may be due to the special doping concentration and oxygen contents. More importantly, we find that the superconducting transition of the grown films are very stable in air. For some films, after being placed in air for more than 1 month (see S1 and S2 in Fig. 1d), apart from a slight increase of the normal-state resistivity, the superconducting transition still looks very sharp without degeneration. Without this kind of heterostructure, the films are pretty easy to deteriorate in air, showing fragility of superconductivity, and it is hard to do the subsequent transport measurements especially under high pressures. However, the LSP327 thin film samples reported here are air-stable, which enables us to conduct subsequent investigation on the transport properties of the bilayer nickelate thin films under pressure in different labs with different high-pressure cells.

Evolution of Tc and normal-state transport behavior under pressures
As reported previously, the superconducting bilayer nickelate thin films were grown on a SLAO substrate with a compressive strain (about −2% compared to bulk crystals), which consequently leads to around +1.5% elongation of the c-axis lattice parameter comparing to bulk samples. This will in turn lead to the elongation of out-of-plane Ni-O bond length, thereby weakening the interlayer d z2-orbital coupling. Naturally, one possible approach to increase Tc in bilayer nickelate thin films is to reduce the c-axis lattice constant through pressure or chemical doping. Figure 2a presents the ρ(T) curves of LSP327 sample (S1) under various pressures up to 2.6 GPa measured in a piston-cylinder cell (PCC) with Daphne 7373 as the pressure transmitting medium (PTM). The normal-state resistivity gradually decreases with increasing pressure, and the residual resistivity at 2 K decreases progressively. As shown in the inset of Fig. 2a, the zero resistance is reached at around 2.3 K above 2.0 GPa, indicating the better connection of the superconducting paths in LSP327 thin films under pressure. The little step at about 173 K at ambient pressure may be due to an instant temperature instability in the warming up process. Figure 2b presents the enlarged view of the ρ(T) curves in the temperature region near the onset of superconducting transitions. The definition of Tonset is illustrated in Fig. 2b. It is clear that the Tonset is monotonically enhanced from 29 to 35.4 K with increasing pressure up to 2.6 GPa, giving a slope dTc/dP of about 2.46 K/GPa. This value is much larger than that reported in the infinite-layer nickelate under high pressure. We have also conducted the transport measurements on another thin film (S2) under high pressure and the results are presented in Supplementary Fig. 4. The similar evolution of ρ(T) curves and Tonset under pressure indicates that the enhancement of superconductivity in the thin films is intrinsic and reproducible.

Figure 2c presents the full range ρ(T) curve of a LSP327 thin film at 2.6 GPa. The curve with red color is the fitting curve using ρ(T) = ρ0 + ATn from Tc to 200 K, and the fitting yields n = 1.79. In the temperature region above 200 K, the ρ(T) curve instead shows a T-linear dependence (n~1) as indicated by the blue line. To see the evolution of the normal-state transport behavior above Tc, we also performed the similar fitting on other ρ(T) curves under different pressures and show the evolution of fitting parameters with pressure in Supplementary Fig. 5. The fitting results indicate that the normal-state transport behavior shows typical Fermi-liquid behavior (n~2), but a slightly decrease of n appear with increasing pressure, which indicates the gradual involvement of other exotic scattering or strange-metal behavior under high pressure. Considering the fact that the strange-metal behavior (n is close to 1) is widely observed in bulk bilayer nickelates under pressure and infinite-layer superconducting films, we may expect that the normal-state resistivity would show a T-linear behavior when the Tc approaches its optimal value. Pressure dependent RH measured at 40 and 60 K shows roughly a declining trend with increasing pressure as displayed in Fig. 2d and Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7. In a single band model, such behavior would indicate that the carrier concentration increases upon applying a pressure. Considering the multi-band nature of bilayer nickelate superconductors and potential role of oxygen deficiency, a quantitative interpretation of the RH data here is very challenging. As we show below, the nonmonotonic change of RH under pressure can be explained by the increasing size of the γ-Fermi pocket with pressure. Anyway, the pressure can indeed enhance the itinerancy of the charge carriers, leading to a better metallicity in the normal state in the pressure region up to 2.6 GPa.

To further study the evolution of Tc in LSP327 bilayer thin film under higher pressures, we performed high-pressure resistivity measurements under various hydrostatic pressures up to 13 GPa using a cubic anvil cell (CAC) apparatus. This technique was successfully used in enhancing the superconducting transition Tc of the infinite-layer nickelate thin films. Figure 3a and Supplementary Fig. 8a show the ρ(T) curves of two LSP327 thin films (S3 and S4) measured with glycerol and Daphne 7373 as the liquid PTM, respectively. The slight variation of absolute resistivity at 0 GPa for different experimental runs is inevitable since there is certain sample dependence in different films, and a slight degradation occurs when polishing the substrate of the thin films for the CAC measurement. Before getting to the enhanced superconductivity under higher pressures, firstly, we focus on the normal-state resistivity above Tc. As shown in Fig. 3a for sample S3, the room temperature resistivity (ρ293K) shows a non-monotonic evolution with increasing pressure, it exhibits a gradual decrease with pressure when P < 7 GPa, and then it shows an increase above 7 GPa. For another sample S4, by using the Daphne 7373 as PTM (see Supplementary Fig. 8), the ρ293K first increases when the pressure is increased from 0 to 2 GPa, and then it decreases with pressure increased from 2 to 4 GPa. With further increasing pressure, it keeps a monotonic increase until 12 GPa. The nonmonotonic change of the normal-state resistivity shows different behavior in different experimental runs (see Supplementary Fig. 9), which is similar to the case in the doped infinite-layer nickelate thin films under high pressures. In these infinite thin films, defects or disorders were observed and are supposed to dominate the electron scattering processes. There are several extrinsic factors that can affect the absolute resistivity of thin films when pressure is applied, for instance, the solidification of PTM, the changes of the electrode contact, defects or disorders generated by pressure, etc. Therefore, we attribute the change of the magnitude of normal-state resistivity in our thin films under pressure to extrinsic reasons. More discussion concerning the abnormal change of normal-state resistivity under pressure can be found in Supplementary Note 2.

Above about 9 GPa, the normal-state resistivity above Tc for experimental runs on two samples (S3 and S4) shows similar metal to weak insulating transitions in low temperature region, and the insulating feature becomes more and more obvious as the pressure is further increased. Despite the variation of normal-state resistive behavior, the superconducting transition can still be clearly observed, which shows an enhancement of Tc with pressure up to around 7 GPa, then it saturates or slightly drops down at higher pressures.

In order to clearly track the evolution of the superconducting transition under high pressures, we show the enlarged view of temperature dependence of resistivity of S3 near onset superconducting transitions and extracted the Tonset at each pressure for samples S3 and S4, as displayed in Fig. 3b–i and Supplementary Fig. 8b–h. We can see that the Tonset exhibits a nonmonotonic evolution with increasing pressure. The definitions of Tonset are the same as that in Fig. 2b. For sample S3, the ρ(T) shows Tonset ≈ 32.4 K at ambient pressure, and the residual resistivity at 1.5 K can be seen clearly, which should be ascribed to the small-sized sample (typical size of 0.6 mm × 0.3 mm) with prominent inhomogeneity for high-pressure measurements. Upon applying pressure to 2 GPa, we can observe perfect zero resistance with Tzero ≈ 2 K and Tonset ≈ 38.3 K for sample S3. The superconducting transition temperature of sample S3 increases to Tonset ≈ 41.3 K and Tzero ≈ 2.4 K at 3.5 GPa, and Tonset ≈ 47.1 K and Tzero ≈ 5.3 K at 5 GPa. With further increasing pressure, we can see that the zero-resistance state cannot be achieved above 7 GPa, but the thin film still exhibits a clear resistivity drop even at 13 GPa. The optimal Tonset ≈ 48.5 K at 7 GPa can be seen in Fig. 3f. We want to note that that if we follow the temperature dependent resistivity curve and determine the temperature where the resistivity starts to drop, the highest temperature of about 61.5 K is observed as shown in the inset of Fig. 3a, which indicates that there is a potential for further optimization of the Tc under pressure in the nickelate bilayer thin films. In contrast, the superconducting transition is considerably broadened with a large residual resistivity for sample S4, and it maybe ascribed to the presence of substantial stress/strain induced by the solidification of Daphne 7373 upon compression and cooling down. However, even the transition becomes broad at high pressures above 9 GPa, we can still track the onset of superconducting transition, and its evolution is consistent with that of sample S3 (see Supplementary Fig. 8). In addition, the slight semiconducting like feature in the normal state above 9 GPa is intriguing. Such a weak insulating behavior seems not be induced by the solidification of the PTM since it occurs in the same way for the two runs of measurements with different PTM (and thus different solidification pressures/temperatures), and this insulating feature was not observed in previous studies on the pressurized effect on the infinite layer thin films, although the PTMs used are the same. We may argue that the weak insulating behavior above Tc at high pressures is an intrinsic property of the bilayer nickelate thin films. The insulating feature occurs at the same pressure when the Tc starts to decrease with pressure and the ρ(T) curves in this region can be fitted by the ρ/-lnT relation (see Supplementary Fig. 10). Such behavior has been reported in the underdoped cuprates. Note that the weak insulating behavior is absent in bulk crystals under pressure, this discrepancy may be because of different electronic structures in bulk samples and thin films. In thin film form of nickelate superconductors, the weak insulating behavior is also observed in Sr-doped La3Ni2O7 with dome-like superconducting region. Therefore, the weak insulating behavior in present bilayer thin films under high pressure maybe induced by some intrinsic origins, for example the gradually enhanced correlation effect which provides the tendency for the formation of a density wave order, probably associated with the shift of the γ-pocket with a flat band feature.

Tc-P phase diagram and theoretical understanding
Figure 4 shows the pressure dependence of superconducting transition Tc obtained from the high-pressure resistive measurements on LSP327 thin films (S1-S4) with different high-pressure cells and PTMs. As can be seen, the phase diagram depicts explicitly a delicate evolution of superconducting transition, which shows clear difference to the results of La3Ni2O7-δ bulk samples. With increasing pressure gradually, Tc(P) shows pronounced positive pressure effect (dTc/dP ~ 3.3 K/GPa) and Tonset exhibits a rapid increase from about 30 K at ambient pressure to 48.5 K at 7 GPa, and then it decreases slowly to 42.8 K at 13 GPa, which features a dome-shaped superconducting phase diagram with the maximum around 7 GPa. The optimal Tonset and the critical pressure in the LSP327 thin films are lower than the corresponding values in its bulk counterpart under a high pressure, which would imply a significant difference of electronic states under pressure in bulk samples and the compressively strained thin films. This can get some reflections from our theoretical analysis as follows.

In Fig. 4, we also mark the behavior of the normal-state resistivity with different colors. Surprisingly, the maximum Tonset corresponds with the threshold pressure for the distinct normal-state behaviors very well, namely the crossover from metallic to weak insulating behavior in low temperature region. Note that the solidification of PTM will not affect the electronic structure of the thin film since it merely introduces disorders or defects in the film, thereby affecting the magnitude of the normal-state resistivity.

To get insight into the electronic origin of the Tc evolution, we first perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations for the strained thin films as a function of pressure. In particular, we assume that external pressure acts on a lattice already clamped by the substrate, so the in-plane lattice constants and the in-plane Ni-O-Ni bond angle remain largely fixed while compression is mostly accommodated along the out-of-plane direction and can be modeled by the variation of the out-of-plane lattice constant c. Thus, our hypothesis is that in thin films pressure mostly affects the c-lattice constant, while keeping in-plane Ni-O-Ni bond angle fixed. More detailed discussion can be found in Supplementary Note 3. On the contrary, in the bulk crystals, there is a remarkable correspondence between the in-plane Ni-O-Ni bond angle and the Tc value once the structural transition to the I4/mmm phase takes place. Note, in compressed thin films the in-plane bond Ni-O angle is more bent than those achieved under hydrostatic pressure, correlating with a lower Tc. Thus, the effect of the hydrostatic pressure on the bulk and thin films is largely different. To be specific, we compute the electronic structure for ambient pressure, c0, and study additionally the cases of 1.5%, 3%, and 5% reduced c by using c = c0 − Δc. In the next step, we develop an effective low-energy model consisting of two 3d x2-y2 and 3d z2-orbitals located on two sites in a bilayer, which is obtained by maximally-localized Wannier downfolding. The three-dimensional effective band structure is only shown for the ambient pressure, as well as the 5% case in Supplementary Fig. 11a. Three bands cross the Fermi level in our model independent of the applied pressure. They are denoted as α, β and γ bands, following the standard nomenclature. The α and β bands are of mixed 3d x2-y2 and 3d z2 orbital character with dominant contribution of the former near the Fermi level. In contrast, the more flattish γ band is of 3d z2 orbital character near the Fermi level. To include the effects of the electronic correlations, we perform the rotationally invariant slave boson approximation, using U=7eV, V=1eV. The renormalized band structures for each pressure are shown in Supplementary Fig. 11b and the resulting Fermi surface for ambient and 5% reduced lattice constant c are shown exemplarily in Fig. 5a. Observe that the largest effect of the pressure for the Fermi surface and the bandwidth occurs for the γ pocket. This is expected due to the strongest effect of the c-lattice variation on the 3d z2 orbital. The γ band shifts upwards with respect to the Fermi level and increases its bandwidth (see Supplementary Fig. 11). This upwards shift corresponds to a charge flow from 3d z2 to 3d x2-y2 orbital with increasing pressure and reflects the reduction of the crystal field splitting (for Δc = c0 = 0, 1.5, 3, 5%: Δcf = 541, 391, 316, 184 meV). The crystal field splitting is also influencing the leading instability in the linearized gap equation based on RPA spin calculations. In addition, we have also performed Hall coefficient calculations within standard Boltzmann theory using the obtained electronic structure (see Supplementary Fig. 12). In the oxygen-rich (clean) case, the Hall coefficient at ambient pressure is slightly negative, consistent with the results of ref. 45. Upon increasing pressure, however, the Hall coefficient turns positive, reflecting the stronger contribution of the γ-band at the Fermi level. This seems to be opposite to the observation of a positive Hall coefficient in our present thin films, which maybe explained by the presence of some oxygen deficiencies in the samples.

In addition, there is an overall increase of itinerancy of the bands, which is due to stronger hybridization of 3d x2-y2 and 3d z2 orbitals and a charge flow from 3d z2 to 3d x2-y2 orbital upon pressure. The increased metallicity is illustrated in Fig. 5b where we plot the quasiparticle weights (residue) of the two orbitals for various pressures. This is consistent with the Hall coefficient data below 2 GPa as shown in Fig. 2d, indicating stronger metallicity of the normal state upon applied pressure. However, the observation of weaking insulating behavior under higher pressure seems contrast to better metallicity proposed from the theoretical results above. As we will discuss below, the weaking insulating behavior may originate from enhanced correlation effect under pressure, namely, the formation of a possible density wave order due to the shift of the γ-pocket with a flat band feature.

Next, we turn to the spin susceptibility as described in Fig. 5 and Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14, and the calculated bare spin susceptibility without doping is depicted in Fig. 5c, d. Both, even (in-plane) and odd (out-of-plane) spin components are shown χe = (χbb + χaa)/2 and χo = (χab + χba)/2. Here, for example, the in-plane χbb describes contributions due to the scattering from a bonding to a bonding band. The odd channel essentially describes the scattering between bonding and antibonding bands. Consequently, strongly dominant spin fluctuations in the odd channel do naturally provide the pairing glue for the bonding-antibonding s±-wave. An enhancement with decreasing c in the odd channel is seen, when the slave boson quasiparticle weights, which are shown in Fig. 5b, are included. Note that the renormalization for the 3d z2 orbital is stronger than that for the 3d x2-y2 orbital. The difference in the orbital renormalization, however, is reduced through reduction of c-axis lattice constant. However, the even spin fluctuations are also significantly sensitive to the changes of the c lattice constant. Especially, a domelike behavior is seen for the qe1 and qe3 peaks, which is consistent with the experimental observation shown in Fig. 4.

Within our theoretical description, the external pressure is modeled by the reduced c-axis lattice constant, while the in-plane lattice constants and the in-plane Ni-O-Ni bond angle remain largely fixed by the substrate. Nevertheless, already this change modifies both the in-plane and the out-of-plane magnetic response, which makes it challenging to single out the main effect responsible for the increase of Tc with pressure and even make further assessment on the most probable symmetry of the superconducting gap. We remind that the main candidate solutions for the superconducting gap in the bilayer nickelates are either bonding-antibonding s±-wave or d-wave (either dxy or dx2-y2) gap structures. At the same time, we can identify universal features in the electronic response upon the reduction of c-axis lattice constant only, which are (i) increased hybridization between 3d z2 and 3d x2-y2 orbitals (ii) larger itinerancy of the pressurized system, and (iii) enhanced antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations both in the in-plane and out-of-plane channels. Moreover, these effects quickly saturate upon larger reduction of the c-axis lattice constant explaining why no further increase of Tc and even its reduction is observed. To see that these universal features stay the same for the slight variation of the electronic structure we repeat the same calculations by doping of 0.1 holes or 0.2 holes per Ni atom assuming potential doping effect of the substrate, as shown in Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14. Remarkably, the universal features we observe for non-doped compound stay the same.

## Methods

Sample preparation and characterization
The nickelate thin films with bilayer structure were grown by pulsed laser deposition technique using (001)-oriented SrLaAlO4 single crystal as substrate. The growth process and parameters are similar to that reported previously. The details about the synthesis process of bilayer heterostructure of La2.5Pr0.5Ni2O7/La2.85Sr0.15Ni2O7 and post annealing parameters are described in Supplementary Note 1. The XRD 2θ-ω scans and RSM were obtained using a Bruker D8 Discover diffractometer with a Cu Kα1 radiation source (λ = 1.5406 Å). The crystal structure was modeled using VESTA software. The temperature-dependent electrical resistivity and Hall coefficient measurements at ambient pressure were carried out on a physical property measurement system (PPMS, Quantum Design) using gold wires as electrodes.

High-pressure measurements in PCC and CAC apparatus
Standard four-probe method was employed to measure temperature-dependent resistivity of the LSP327 thin films with the electric current applied within the ab-plane. Resistivity measurements with pressures below 2.6 GPa were carried out in a PCC apparatus (HPC-33, Quantum Design). The sample was immersed in a liquid PTM of Daphne 7373 in a Teflon cell. Hydrostatic pressures were generated by a non magnetic BeCu/NiCrAl piston-cylinder cell. The applied pressure at low temperature was determined by the shift in Tc of a high quality Pb single crystal. The Hall resistance at ambient and high pressures (below 2.6 GPa) was measured using a five-probe method and the electrode configuration is shown in the inset of Fig. 1c. For measurements at higher pressures, we employ a palm-type CAC to measure its resistivity under various pressures up to 13 GPa with the glycerol as the liquid PTM, and to 12 GPa with the Daphne 7373 as the liquid PTM. The pressure values inside the CAC were estimated from the pressure-loading force calibration curve pre-determined by measuring the Bi and Pb at low temperatures. The resistivity values in CAC at 0 GPa is a little bit larger than that in PCC at ambient pressure, this may be due to the slight degradation of the film when we polish the substrate of the thin film to lower its thickness for the CAC measurements.

Theoretical calculation
To get insights into the electronic states of the thin films, DFT in the local density approximation within a mixed-basis pseudopotential framework is applied. The application of pressure is modeled by variation of the out-of-plane lattice constant and fixed in-plane lattice constant within a bulk-like setting. To be specific, we use c0 for ambient pressure and study additionally the cases of 1.5%, 3% and 5% reduced c by using c = c0 − Δc, while keeping the in-plane parameters fixed.

In bilayer systems, the electronic states in band space can be approximately diagonalized by introducing bonding and antibonding states c±,k = 1/√2 (c1,k ± c2,k), where c1,k and c2,k denote the annihilation operators for an electron in layer 1 and 2 with momentum k, respectively. Within the description of the two orbital bilayer model, the α and γ bands belong to the bonding subspace whereas the β band is of antibonding character. Scattering events can be classified in those which happen within the bonding or antibonding bands and those which happen between both subspaces. The even and odd susceptibilities are defined by χe,o = 2(χ11,11 ± χ11,22), where orbital and spin indices are omitted. The physical spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic state is determined by even and odd channels as χspin(q) = Σμ1,μ2,μ3,μ4 [χeμ1μ1,μ2μ2(q)cos2(qz/2) + χoμ1μ1,μ2μ2(q)sin2(qz/2)], where q = (q, ω) and the sum μ1,2 run over both Ni eg orbitals. The bare susceptibility is calculated using the renormalized band structure. Furthermore, the slave-boson quasi-particle weight is dominated by the diagonal part. These diagonal elements Zμ can be used as Zμ1 Zμ2 Zμ3 Zμ4 χe,oμ1μ1,μ2μ2(q) to account for the orbital selective quasiparticle weights. While the spin susceptibility is only shown along the high-symmetry path in the qz = 0 plane, the full k dependence of the band structure is included in the calculation. To be specific, a 200×200×25 k-mesh and bulk filling has been used to obtain the results in Fig. 5. To account for the possibility of hole doping, the calculations were repeated for 0.1 and 0.2 holes per Ni atom. The results are shown in Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14. The discussed trends are similar for all doping. In addition, we computed the quasiparticle contribution to the longitudinal, transverse conductivities, including the individual band contributions and the total Hall coefficient at T = 60 K using the previously developed Kubo formalism for correlated electrons and the results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 12.

### Reviewer 2

This is an excellent manuscript with a significant contribution to the field of high-temperature superconductivity in nickelates
La3Ni2O7. The authors successfully demonstrate a pressure-induced enhancement of superconductivity in compressively
strained thin film samples, revealing a dome-shaped T-P phase diagram. The combination of high-quality experimental data
and insightful theoretical analysis provides a compelling case for the proposed mechanism. I believe this work is highly
suitable for publication and recommend its acceptance following a thorough and careful revision based on the following
comments.
(1). The observation of a transition from metallic to weak insulating behavior at pressures above the optimal 9 GPa is a
critical and intriguing finding. To fully substantiate this phenomenon and provide deeper insight, a more detailed analysis is
required. It would be invaluable to see the full resistance-temperature curves at pressures both below and above this
transition point. A discussion on whether this behavior is linked to an intrinsic structural or electronic phase transition, such
as a charge density wave or Fermi surface reconstruction, would be highly valuable. Are there any other signatures or
characteristics of this weak insulating behavior (e.g., a change in the resistance slope, hysteretic behavior, or
magnetoresistance behavior) that could provide additional insights? Providing a more detailed picture of the normal state
properties in this high-pressure regime will greatly strengthen the manuscript's conclusions.
(2). The manuscript attributes the enhanced superconductivity to a synergy of enhanced orbital hybridization, improved
itinerancy, and stronger magnetic fluctuations. While the qualitative argument is sound, a more quantitative or at least
qualitative analysis distinguishing the relative importance of these factors would be a significant addition. Furthermore, given
the discussion of magnetic fluctuations as the likely pairing glue, a brief discussion on the likely symmetry of the
superconducting pairing (e.g., d-wave or s-wave) and how it evolves under pressure, or a future outlook on this topic, would be
highly beneficial for a comprehensive understanding.
(3). The theoretical model assumes that applied hydrostatic pressure primarily reduces the out-of-plane lattice constant, with
the in-plane constant clamped by the substrate.
However, smaller in-plane lattice constant would also influence the electronic behavior, e.g., leading to enhanced intralayer
interorbital hybridization. Could the authors provide a quantitative estimate of the actual strain state of the film under
pressure? A more detailed justification for the assumption of a fixed in-plane lattice parameter would strengthen the
connection between the theoretical model and experimental conditions.
(4). The Hall effect measurements indicate that the primary charge carriers are holes and that their density slightly increases
with pressure. To substantiate this claim, it would be highly beneficial to include specific numerical data or estimations of the
carrier concentration at various pressures. Additionally, the manuscript would be significantly enhanced by a qualitative
discussion on how the theoretically predicted alpha, beta, and gamma bands, which are believed to cross the Fermi level,
evolve under pressure. Specifically, which of these bands is most responsible for the observed hole-like nature of the
carriers, and what is its role in contributing to superconductivity? This discussion would offer deeper insights into the
microscopic electronic structure.
(5). The manuscript could benefit from a brief discussion on the potential influence of the interlayer Ni-O-Ni bond angle, as
this factor has been shown to be crucial in other nickelate studies and may be relevant to the observed interlayer spin
fluctuations.
(6). There are minor inconsistencies between some figures and the main text. For example, the peak of the superconducting
dome in Figure 4 (nearly 7.5 GPa) appears slightly different from the value stated (9 GPa) in the text. While the regime
plotting in Figure 4 is only approximate, it will still be helpful to make the phase diagram more consistent with the text.

### Reviewer 3

Li et al. presents a comprehensive investigation of enhanced superconductivity in compressively strained bilayer nickelate
thin films under hydrostatic pressure. The authors demonstrate that the superconducting transition temperature can be
enhanced from ~40 K at ambient pressure to over 61.5 K at 9 GPa, revealing a dome-shaped pressure-temperature phase
diagram. The study combines experimental work with theoretical calculations to provide insights into the underlying
mechanisms. Overall, the study addresses an important topic in the rapidly evolving field of nickelate superconductivity and
the results are generally well presented.
I recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications after addressing the following questions and
suggestions:
1. Heterostructure design rationale: The authors employ a heterostructure design with 1.5 UC of La2.5Pr0.5Ni2O7 and 1.5
UC of La2.85Sr0.15Ni2O7 to enhance stability, but the specific choice of Sr doping concentration (x=0.15) and layer
thicknesses appears somewhat arbitrary. Could the authors provide more detailed justification for these parameters? Were
systematic studies conducted to optimize these values, or were they based on prior literature? Please provide more
information.
2. Strain characterization limitations: While the authors claim compressive strain based on c-axis elongation from XRD 2θ-ω
scans, this characterization is insufficient for a heterostructure containing two different compositions with potentially different
lattice parameters. Reciprocal space mapping (RSM) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM) would provide more
definitive evidence of the strain state and film quality. The current XRD data quality also appears limited for making strong
claims about crystalline quality.
3. Hall coefficient interpretation: The positive Hall coefficients observed in this work contrast with recent literature reports
showing negative Hall coefficients in Sr-doped bilayer nickelate films. Given that this heterostructure contains both Sr and
Pr, could the authors provide a more detailed discussion of the charge carrier behaviour and how it relates to the
superconducting mechanism in their specific system?
4. Data presentation: The resistance vs. temperature data should be converted to resistivity vs. temperature for proper
materials characterization and cross-comparison with others’ work. Additionally, experimental uncertainties should be
included, particularly for the transition temperatures in the phase diagram.
5. Mechanisms: The manuscript describes two different trends in superconducting transition behaviour under pressure but
does not clearly explain their origins. Could the authors elaborate on what physical mechanisms drive these different
behaviours and how they relate to the theoretical calculations?
6. Reproducibility: While multiple samples are measured, it would be valuable to include a more quantitative discussion of
sample-to-sample variation in superconducting properties at ambient pressure, particularly given the complexity of the
heterostructure growth and post-annealing process.
Despite these questions, this work represents a significant contribution to understanding pressure effects in nickelate
superconductors and successfully demonstrates substantial enhancement of transition temperatures through the
combination of strain engineering and pressure tuning.

nickelate films we emulate applied pressure by compressing the out-of-plane
lattice parameter c while keeping the in-plane lattice constant a fixed at its
ambient pressure value. This choice reflects the experimental geometry: the
film is epitaxially clamped to a rigid substrate so the in-plane lattice is set by the

film is free to change its interlayer spacing. Physically, the dominant pressure-

relaxations. Computationally, fixing a while fully relaxing internal coordinates for

freedom affected by pressure, and it also allows straightforward comparison to
film experiments where in-plane clamping is present.

3. The theoretical model assumes that applied hydrostatic pressure primarily

Response: This remark is similar to the comment 12 of the Referee #1. As
pointed above, in the bulk crystals there is a remarkable correspondence

c
transition to the I4/mmm phase takes place, see for example Fig.1 in B.
Samanta, and A.B. Georgescu, arXiv: 2506.11427. This means that it is the in-

c
strained thin films, the situation is different, external pressure acts on a lattice
already clamped by the substrate (especially there are only few unit cells in thin

remain largely fixed (here we refer again to the arXiv:2506.11427), while
compression is mostly accommodated along the out-of-plane direction. Along
the c-axis, there is the bilayer segment and the LaO spacer segment and
therefore much more susceptible to changes with pressure. The smaller, and
thus "more homogeneous", a-axis with the stiff transition metal-O bonds is not

Response: We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We followed the
Referee’s recommendation and present in Fig. R5 the calculated Hall
coefficient, modeled within a quasiparticle approximation to the electronic
states, as a function of pressure. At ambient pressure, the Hall coefficient is
small and negative, in remarkable agreement with the values reported for
oxygen-rich samples by Maosen Wang et al. (arXiv:2508.15284). With
increasing pressure, the Hall coefficient changes sign and becomes positive,
reflecting the enhanced contribution of the hole-like γ pocket at the Fermi level
and a stronger tendency toward s± superconductivity.
Experimentally, however, we consistently observe a positive Hall coefficient.
By having a comparison with Ref. 45 [Maosen Wang et al., arXiv:2508.15284],
this suggests the presence of a certain degree of oxygen deficiency (interstitials)
in our samples. Since the α and β bands contribute with opposite signs to the
Hall coefficient and the γ-band contribution is relatively small, oxygen deficiency
may dominate the pressure evolution of the Hall response. Consequently, the
experimental Hall data should not be interpreted solely as a direct signature of
electronic structure evolution under pressure. To achieve a more conclusive
analysis, studies on next-generation, higher-quality films will be required.

with the reviewer that the interlayer Ni-O-Ni bond angle is crucial for the
occurrence of superconductivity in nickelates. However, at this moment, we
cannot do the synchrotron diffraction measurement on the thin films under
pressure to determine the Ni-O-Ni bond angle. The in-plane lattice is
determined at ambient pressure to be about 3.75 Å, which is about -2% strained
compared with the bulk value. The c-axis lattice constant is accordingly
elongated. Since the thin films are already superconductive at ambient pressure,
the Ni-O-Ni bond angle was supposed to be close to 180as the bulk samples
in the tetragonal phase. Under pressures, we may expect that the Ni-O-Ni bond
length will shrink.
In theoretical modeling we assume a full tetragonal symmetry of the system.
Note that the effects of finite Ni-O-Ni bond angle is discussed extensively by B.
Samanta, and A.B. Georgescu, arXiv: 2506.11427 and we include the reference
to their paper for consistency.
In the revised manuscript, we have some discussion on the interlayer Ni-
O-Ni bond angle under pressure and its possible relations to the interlayer spin
fluctuations. We hope the reviewer will satisfied with those reversions and
discussions.
